title: The Tirpitz goes down
pull: Twelve thousand pounds, dropped from the sky

facts.text: On the morning of 12 November 1944, RAF Lancaster bombers of No. 9 and No. 617 Squadrons, led by Wing Commander J. B. Tait, attacked the German battleship Tirpitz near Tromso, in the far north of Norway.
Each Lancaster carried a single Tallboy, a 12,000 pound deep penetration bomb.
Sources give between 29 and 32 bombers. They scored at least two direct hits and more near misses.
The bombers began their run at 09:35. Within minutes the ship was listing hard, and after a magazine exploded she rolled over and capsized.
Somewhere between about 950 and 1,204 German sailors died. The RAF Museum puts it at about a thousand.
Men trapped inside the upturned hull were cut free through her exposed bottom; 82 were rescued that way.
Tirpitz displaced about 42,900 tonnes and carried eight 15 inch guns. She had hardly fought, but simply by existing she forced the Royal Navy to keep powerful forces in home waters to watch her.
Britain had tried for years to sink her: midget submarines in September 1943, carrier dive bombers in April 1944, and Lancasters with Tallboys in September 1944.
An Australian film crew from No. 463 Squadron RAAF flew with the raid and filmed the attack and the end of the ship.
With Tirpitz gone, the last German battleship threat to the Arctic convoys and the North Atlantic was over.

declassified.fact: The Tallboy was designed by Barnes Wallis. Dropped on concrete it could bore up to five meters down before it went off, and its shock wave did most of the damage. That is why near misses could still wreck a battleship.
